Resources and methods

Current story: WIC, from eligibility to groceries. Reviewed September 2026. This investigation synthesizes published evidence; it does not include original interviews.

National estimates, local qualitative accounts, state rules, and benefit-redemption studies answer different questions. They are not stages of one measured dropout funnel.

Restored receipt comparison

The current story again includes the seven-item basket: $22.63 total, $19.14 paid by WIC, and $3.49 paid by the household, assuming sufficient issued benefits and the recorded approved products. Brown eggs are a rule comparison only. Prices and products · Recorded product matches. The repeated-basket savings and archived balance below are not used in the current story.

Archived examples and earlier research

The material below documents the earlier version, including its hypothetical grocery basket. It is preserved for reference and is not part of the current narrative.

The household and conversations are illustrative. National participation estimates, local research, California food rules, and the example transaction have different populations and dates.

The shopping example

The story uses an example California child food package for an eligible four-year-old. The FY2026 baseline $26 produce allowance is additional to food quantities. Optional substitutions change the package and are not added on top of the baseline here. The verified basket totals $22.63 before tax: $19.14 paid by WIC and $3.49 household-paid, assuming approved products and sufficient benefits. Published retailer prices were observed September 20, 2026; the story illustrates an in-store transaction, not WIC payment online.

The same groceries appear in both payment scenarios. The example does not represent a named person or establish what a nonparticipating household would go without. No annual use rate or medical outcome is invented.

Repeated-basket calculations use one identical basket monthly at fixed prices and continued qualifying coverage: 12 × $19.14 = $229.68; 48 × $19.14 = $918.72. These are not typical savings or the full package’s value.

Map

The current store-access scene uses USDA’s FY2022 proximity analysis: 40% of estimated WIC-eligible families in the 50 states and DC lacked convenient retailer access. Thresholds are one driving mile in urban areas and ten in rural areas, measured from population-weighted census-tract centers. Families below 185% of poverty with children under five are the eligibility proxy. This is not a measured household commute. The route download below is retained as an archived illustration from an earlier version.

California’s reporting snapshot is separate from national 2023 estimates. Associations do not establish causality; age groups are not a tracked cohort. Illustrations were generated for this story and composed with existing artwork; all labels and numbers are live webpage text.

September 22 additions: states, reasons, and household examples

State tiles and counts reproduce USDA Table 3.5, CY2023. Each rate uses its own estimated eligible population; the selector shows the 95% interval. State differences are not isolated policy effects. The national people graphic rounds 56.1% participation to 56 filled figures out of 100, with 44 outlined figures; exact figures remain in its labels.

Awareness percentages (23.3% and 22.6%) describe current adult participants explaining non-enrollment during earlier pregnancies, from USDA’s 2019 survey, Exhibit 4. The separate 59% perceived-need finding comes from a convenience sample of 125 former participants. Neither explains a measured share of the 2023 national gap.

Reasons for unused benefits draw on 37 Massachusetts caregiver interviews in 2020–2021. These qualitative themes are separate from the Southern California redemption estimates.

The stock-up basket triples milk, apples, and peas quantities at the original regular unit prices, keeping other products at one each: $42.97 total, $39.48 WIC-covered food, $3.49 household payment. Quantities fit the relevant options in the California child package guide, assuming enough issued benefits. It is not a full monthly package. Optional six/twelve-month comparisons multiply one identical purchase per month: small basket $114.84/$229.68; stock-up $236.88/$473.76. They assume continued eligibility, new monthly benefits and unchanged prices. No typical savings or rollover claim is made.

The benefits finder routes to government resources using selected needs and household situations. It does not determine eligibility. Only WIC includes an optional basic federal income comparison, based on July 2026–June 2027 guidelines, with Alaska/Hawaii adjustments and additional-member increments. This comparison stops after the guidelines expire. No other program is filtered out based on income. Answers are neither stored nor sent.
